title: Salience Effect
hook: One bright detail can drag a whole decision off balance while the dull facts sit untouched.
counterintuition: The detail you notice first may be the least important one; name its salience, then force the choice back through base importance.
tryThisNow: Pick one decision with a vivid detail attached. Write that detail at the top, then list the three dull facts that should carry more weight.
keyTakeaway: Salience makes a vivid feature look important because it is easy to notice. Treat brightness as a warning to check the quieter base facts.

breakdown.fastRead: The policy draft in the coffee supplier deal has a photo of split burlap sacks on the cover. Francis keeps looking at it while the shipping terms sit on page four. Salience makes the vivid detail feel like the main risk. He writes salience beside the photo, moves the freight record to the first score line, and makes the buyer choose by base importance, not by the loudest image.
breakdown.deepRead:
Attention is not a fair judge. It grabs what is bright, recent, emotional, unusual, or easy to picture. Once attention grabs a feature, the mind often treats that feature as if it must deserve the weight it receives.

The salience effect is this slide from noticeable to important. A neonatal team may remember one dramatic oxygen-line error and rewrite a checklist around that vivid detail while a dull infection-control step causes more harm each month. A flood insurance clerk may focus on a spectacular airport delay photo and miss the boring map layer that actually changes the household's risk. The eye is not the same as the scale.

Bright is not the same as important.

The correction is to mark the vivid detail before it becomes the decision. Name it: salience. Then ask what the base importance would be if the detail were printed in gray. Which factor changes outcomes most often? Which risk has the largest cost? Which number would matter if nobody had seen the photo, heard the story, or watched the clip?

This is not a call to ignore vivid evidence. Sometimes the bright detail is bright because it is a real warning. A site photo of ice at a shelter entrance may reveal a danger that the spreadsheet missed. The move is to test the detail against base importance, not to let it skip the test.
breakdown.fullRead:
The site photo in the winter shelter allocation shows a blue tarp whipping loose in a freezing wind. Esther, the housing coordinator, can feel the room move toward that site before anyone has compared bed counts, transit access, or staffing. The photo matters. It may show a genuine problem. But if it becomes the whole decision, salience has replaced the allocation rule.

Salient information has unfair access to the mind. It is easy to recall, easy to describe, and easy to defend in a meeting. Quiet information has to work harder. Base rates, average costs, failure frequency, and long-term capacity rarely sparkle. They arrive as columns, not scenes.

Which fact would still matter if it had no photograph?

De Bondt and Thaler's Do Analysts Overreact put this pressure into the world of markets and forecasts. Analysts can become too responsive to striking news or vivid recent information, even when base importance and longer patterns deserve more weight. The lesson travels beyond finance: a bright feature pulls judgment toward what can be seen, retold, or emotionally replayed.

That pull can be useful. A vivid detail can break complacency. A neonatal floor sticker that keeps getting peeled back may reveal that a safety route is not as clear as the checklist says. A goalkeeper academy's blood-test panel may flag a fatigue issue that coaches cannot see during drills. Salience becomes a problem when the feature wins because it is vivid, not because it changes the outcome that matters.

The quiet facts need a chair at the table.

A newsroom front-page meeting shows the trap cleanly. A loan worksheet contains one heartbreaking borrower quote, and the room wants the story above the fold. The quote is real. It should not be erased. But the editor still has to compare public impact, novelty, evidence strength, and who is affected. A vivid quote can open attention. It should not decide placement by itself.

The practical correction is a salience brake. First, put the vivid detail in a box and label it. Second, list the base facts that should matter even without the vivid item. Third, decide how much the detail should change the weights. If it reveals a hidden variable, raise its weight. If it only adds color, keep it from taking over.

The limit is that decisions need human attention. You cannot run a city, ward, fund, or newsroom on blank tables alone. People notice what they can see, and vivid detail often carries human truth that averages flatten. The error is not noticing. The error is letting notice become rank.

Before the next choice moves forward, ask what is loud and what is large. The loud thing may deserve action, but it has to earn its place beside the large thing. Once salience is named, the bright feature stops choosing for the room.

examples.title: Francis moves the freight line up
examples.scenario: A policy draft sits beside three green coffee sample bags in a Rotterdam supplier negotiation at 2:30 p.m. Francis must decide whether to reject a farm cooperative after seeing a photo of split burlap sacks on the cover. He writes salience beside the photo, moves freight reliability and defect rate to the first comparison line, and changes the supplier vote in front of the buyer.
examples.whatToDo: Label the striking photo as salience, then force the supplier choice through freight reliability and defect rates before the vote.
examples.whyItMatters: The torn-sack image may be real, but it can crowd out the quieter terms that decide cost, delivery, and quality over the contract.

planSpec.domain: a coffee supplier negotiation applying Salience Effect under operational pressure

examples.title: Esther checks the dull checklist line
examples.scenario: "That sticker is impossible to miss," the nurse says during a neonatal checklist review in Calgary at 7:05 a.m. A bright floor sticker marks the resuscitation route, but Esther must decide whether the vivid detail should outrank the quieter infection-control miss rate. She circles vivid detail on the sticker, adds the miss rate beside it, and changes the next checklist revision in front of the charge nurse.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the vivid sticker visible, but make the checklist revision compare it with the higher-frequency infection-control risk.
examples.whyItMatters: The sticker gets attention because it is visible. The checklist should follow harm and frequency, not only the detail everyone remembers.

planSpec.domain: a neonatal checklist review applying Salience Effect under operational pressure

examples.title: Geoffrey weighs the shelter photo
examples.scenario: The site photo is cold enough to feel wet in the winter shelter allocation room in Ottawa at 5:45 p.m. Geoffrey must decide whether the tarp-flapping image should move one site ahead of another with more beds and better transit. He marks base importance on the photo, asks the planner to read capacity aloud, and changes the allocation sheet only after the larger factors are scored.
examples.whatToDo: Use the photo as a risk cue, then score bed count, transit, staffing, and exposure before moving the shelter site.
examples.whyItMatters: A bleak image can dominate the room while capacity affects more people. Base importance keeps visible hardship from swallowing total impact.

planSpec.domain: a winter shelter allocation applying Salience Effect under operational pressure

examples.title: Avril slows the academy drill
examples.scenario: You are holding a blood-test panel at a goalkeeper academy in Lyon while a teenager's spectacular diving save loops on the training screen. Avril, the performance coach, must decide whether the save should keep him in the drill despite fatigue markers. She writes attention on the panel, shows the marker to the head coach, and changes the drill list before the next set begins.
examples.whatToDo: Put the eye-catching save beside the fatigue marker, then choose the drill list from injury risk and training load.
examples.whyItMatters: The save wins attention, but the blood-test panel may carry the larger risk. Salience should not decide who trains through fatigue.

planSpec.domain: a goalkeeper academy drill applying Salience Effect under operational pressure

examples.title: Anne separates flood risk from delay drama
examples.scenario: It took Anne one claims season in Hamburg to see that the flood insurance desk kept overreacting to the airport board photo after every storm delay. She predicted clients would need air-travel riders, but the reveal was basement loss data. Before renewing the brochure, she must decide whether the vivid feature belongs on page one or behind the flood-zone map.
examples.whatToDo: Mark the airport board as a salient feature, then rank brochure space by claim frequency, loss size, and flood-zone exposure.
examples.whyItMatters: Travel disruption is easy to picture, but flood exposure drives the actual insurance need. The feature should not outrank the base loss data.

planSpec.domain: a flood insurance desk applying Salience Effect under operational pressure

examples.title: Christopher's front-page postmortem
examples.scenario: Which deserved the front page: the heartbreaking quote or the larger pattern? Christopher asks that after a newsroom meeting in Cardiff reviews a loan worksheet from the previous night's housing story. The vivid quote drove placement while the broader lending data sat lower. He marks effect on the worksheet and changes the next meeting so impact, novelty, and evidence strength are scored before quotes are read.
examples.whatToDo: Let vivid quotes open the discussion only after the front-page criteria have been scored from evidence and public impact.
examples.whyItMatters: A quote can focus attention without proving rank. Scoring the larger criteria first keeps salience from choosing the lead story.

reviewCards.front: A vivid detail grabs the room. What base rate should regain attention?
reviewCards.back: Bring back the base rate, total scale, and less vivid evidence. Salient details need a denominator.
Ask which factor changes outcomes most often, at the largest scale, or at the highest cost.

reviewCards.front: When can a salient detail deserve weight?
reviewCards.back: When it reveals a hidden variable or changes the expected outcome, not merely because it is memorable.

reviewCards.front: A photo, quote, or clip is driving the decision. What is the correction?
reviewCards.back: Label it as salient, list the base facts, then decide how much the detail should change the weights.

reviewCards.front: Why do dull facts lose in meetings?
reviewCards.back: They arrive as columns instead of scenes, so they need a deliberate place in the choice structure.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Label the vivid feature, list the quieter base facts, and choose by weighted importance instead of attention.

ifThenPlans.plan: If one image dominates the packet, then I will move reliability, cost, and failure rates above it before deciding.
If one dramatic incident leads the room, then I will compare severity, frequency, and preventability before changing protocol.
If one quote carries the room, then I will score impact and evidence before choosing placement.
If a vivid disruption story grabs attention, then I will check claim frequency and loss size before allocating space or money.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one vivid detail that influenced you today. Write the base facts it may have crowded out and decide whether it truly changes their weight.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review a decision where the loudest detail won and ask what the quiet largest factor was.

memorableLines.text: Bright is not the same as important.
The quiet facts need a chair at the table.
